subject: Environment
topic: NGT and environmental laws — mixed tiers
description: National Green Tribunal, EIA, CRZ, Forest Rights Act

questions.stem: The National Green Tribunal was set up under the NGT Act of:
questions.explanation: The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 replaced the earlier National Environment Tribunal (1995) and National Environment Appellate Authority (1997). NGT became operational on 18 October 2010. Principal bench at Delhi; regional benches at Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai. Cases must be filed within 6 months of cause of action. Appeals go to the Supreme Court, not the High Court.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven laws the National Green Tribunal has jurisdiction over?

options.option_text: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
Right to Information Act, 2005
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
Biological Diversity Act, 2002

questions.explanation: NGT has jurisdiction under seven specific environmental laws listed in Schedule I: Water Act 1974, Water Cess Act 1977, Forest Conservation Act 1980, Air Act 1981, Environment (Protection) Act 1986, Public Liability Insurance Act 1991, Biological Diversity Act 2002. RTI 2005 is a transparency law, not an environmental one, and sits outside NGT's remit. Wildlife Protection Act 1972 is also not in Schedule I — wildlife cases go to the regular courts.

questions.stem: Under the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification, which zone carries the strictest restrictions on construction?

options.option_text: CRZ-I
CRZ-II
CRZ-III
CRZ-IV

questions.explanation: CRZ-I covers ecologically sensitive areas — mangroves, coral reefs, turtle nesting grounds, salt marshes — and the inter-tidal zone itself. Development is virtually banned. CRZ-II covers built-up urban coastal areas (Mumbai seafront, Chennai Marina). CRZ-III covers rural / relatively undisturbed coasts. CRZ-IV is the water area from the low-tide line up to 12 nautical miles out. The CRZ notification is issued under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

questions.stem: The principle 'polluter pays' was incorporated into Indian environmental jurisprudence by the Supreme Court in which landmark case?

options.option_text: Olga Tellis vs Bombay Municipal Corporation
Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action vs Union of India
Vishaka vs State of Rajasthan
Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum vs Union of India

questions.explanation: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action vs UoI (1996) — the Bichhri tank case — applied the 'polluter pays' principle, holding H Acid Plant chemical firms strictly liable for damage caused by their effluents. The Vellore Citizens case (also 1996) further developed the precautionary principle. Olga Tellis (1985) was on pavement dwellers' right to life. Vishaka (1997) laid down workplace sexual-harassment guidelines.

questions.stem: An Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) in India is required before approving:

options.option_text: Any commercial activity
Specified development projects listed in the EIA Notification schedules
Only foreign-funded projects
Projects only above ₹500 crore

questions.explanation: EIA Notification 2006 (most recent major revision; a draft 2020 notification is still pending) lists projects in two categories: Category A (central government clearance) and Category B (state-level). Trigger examples — thermal plants > 50 MW, mines above 5 ha, highways, airports, ports, industrial estates > 500 ha. Below-threshold projects don't need EIA. Public hearing is one stage of the process; the Expert Appraisal Committee recommends approval.

questions.stem: The Forest Rights Act, 2006 recognises the rights of forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers over forest resources. The Act also gives the Gram Sabha which key power?

options.option_text: Levy property tax on forest dwellers
Consent over diversion of forest land for non-forest projects
Appoint forest officers directly
Override Supreme Court orders on forests

questions.explanation: Under the Forest Rights Act (FRA) 2006, the Gram Sabha is the authority that initiates recognition of individual and community forest rights. Its consent is required for any diversion of forest land for non-forest purposes in Scheduled V areas (upheld in Niyamgiri / Vedanta case, 2013). This is distinct from PESA 1996, which gives Gram Sabhas in Fifth-Schedule areas broader planning powers. FRA's implementing ministry is Tribal Affairs, not Environment.

questions.stem: The 'Extended Producer Responsibility' (EPR) concept has been incorporated into Indian rules covering:

options.option_text: Drinking water quality
Plastic, e-waste and battery waste management
Air pollution
Noise pollution

questions.explanation: EPR makes the producer responsible for the end-of-life management of their product's packaging or waste. India has EPR under — Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 (amended 2022), E-Waste Management Rules 2022, Battery Waste Management Rules 2022. Producers must register with CPCB and meet annual collection / recycling targets. Extended producer responsibility is a polluter-pays variant aimed at incentivising better product design.

questions.stem: The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 was enacted to give effect to resolutions adopted at which international event, as explicitly stated in its Preamble?

options.option_text: Stockholm Conference on Human Environment, 1972
Rio Earth Summit on Sustainable Development, 1992
Kyoto Protocol negotiations on climate change, 1997
Nairobi Convention on Ozone Layer Protection, 1985

questions.explanation: A is correct because the Preamble of the Air Act, 1981 explicitly references decisions taken at the UN Conference on the Human Environment held at Stockholm in June 1972. The Rio Summit (1992) and Kyoto Protocol (1997) post-date the Act's enactment, making them chronologically impossible distractors. Nairobi 1985 is a fabricated convention reference.

questions.stem: The National Green Tribunal (NGT) has its Principal Bench seated at which city, from which all suo motu and writ-jurisdiction matters are typically heard?

options.option_text: Mumbai, the country's commercial and financial hub
New Delhi, the seat of the Union Government
Chennai, which hosts the Southern Zone circuit bench
Bhopal, which hosts the Central Zone circuit bench

questions.explanation: B is correct because the NGT Act, 2010 and subsequent government notifications establish New Delhi as the seat of the NGT's Principal Bench. Chennai and Bhopal host circuit benches (Southern and Central Zones respectively), a common source of confusion. Mumbai has no NGT bench — the Western Zone bench sits at Pune.

questions.stem: Under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, which body serves as the apex national authority for regulating access to biological resources and associated traditional knowledge, and where is it headquartered?

options.option_text: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
State Biodiversity Boards constituted by state governments
National Biodiversity Authority, headquartered in Chennai
Biodiversity Management Committees at the local body level

questions.explanation: C is correct because Section 8 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 establishes the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA), headquartered in Chennai, as the apex body. State Biodiversity Boards and Biodiversity Management Committees are subordinate tiers operating at state and local levels respectively; the MoEFCC is the parent ministry, not the regulatory authority itself.

questions.stem: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 was enacted by Parliament primarily as a legislative response to which trigger event or need?

options.option_text: Severe flooding in the Brahmaputra basin in northeastern India
The need to implement Stockholm Conference resolutions of 1972
Recommendations of the Tiwari Committee on environmental laws
The Bhopal gas tragedy caused by methyl isocyanate leak

questions.explanation: D is correct because the Bhopal gas disaster of December 1984 — the world's worst industrial chemical accident — exposed a glaring gap in India's environmental law and provided the immediate political impetus for the EPA 1986. Option B is tempting since the EPA Preamble does cite Stockholm (1972), but that was a background motivation, not the primary trigger. The Tiwari Committee did recommend such legislation, but Bhopal gave it urgency.

questions.stem: Under the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017, which body is designated as the regulatory authority for wetlands located entirely within a state territory?

options.option_text: State Wetland Authority constituted by the state government
Central Wetlands Regulatory Authority under Ministry of Jal Shakti
National Green Tribunal through suo motu powers under NGT Act
District Wetland Committee headed by the District Magistrate

questions.explanation: A is correct because Rule 4 of the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 mandates each state government to constitute a State Wetland Authority as the competent regulatory body for wetlands within the state. No 'Central Wetlands Regulatory Authority' exists under the Rules — that is a misleading analogy with CPCB. NGT has appellate/suo motu jurisdiction, not primary regulatory authority under these Rules.

questions.stem: The Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016 implement India's obligations under which convention specifically governing the cross-border movement of hazardous waste?

options.option_text: Rotterdam Convention on prior informed consent for chemicals
Minamata Convention on mercury and mercury-containing products
Stockholm Convention on persistent organic pollutants globally
Basel Convention on transboundary movements of hazardous wastes

questions.explanation: D is correct because the Basel Convention (1989), ratified by India in 1992, is the treaty that specifically regulates transboundary movement and disposal of hazardous wastes, and the 2016 Rules operationalise it domestically. Rotterdam Convention covers Prior Informed Consent for certain hazardous chemicals in international trade; Stockholm targets persistent organic pollutants; Minamata deals exclusively with mercury — all plausible but wrong in this specific context.

questions.stem: Under Section 16 of the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, what is the limitation period for filing an application for relief or compensation before the NGT, and what discretionary extension is available?

options.option_text: Three months, extendable by sixty days on sufficient cause shown
Six months, extendable by sixty days on showing sufficient cause
One year, extendable by a further one year for sufficient cause
Two years, with no provision for condonation of delay at all

questions.explanation: B is correct because Section 16 of the NGT Act, 2010 prescribes six months from the date on which the cause of action first arose, with a proviso allowing the Tribunal to condone delay by up to sixty days on showing sufficient cause. Candidates often confuse this with the standard 1-year or 3-year periods under the Limitation Act, 1963, which does not govern NGT proceedings. 'Three months' refers to no specific NGT provision; 'two years with no extension' inverts the actual position.
